wine.name: Grand Vintage
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, about two thirds in the releases read, with Pinot Noir for the rest.
wine.sites: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir drawn from vineyards across the island's cool districts and woven into one blend, the idea behind the house's name, a word for tapestry.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle, then held on its lees, the house's tirage, for years before disgorging: six years and more for the 2015, 2016 and 2017 and nine for the 2009 by the house's own pages. The dosage is kept low.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, lemon curd and oyster shell over brioche, roasted almond and nougat from the long lees ageing; a fine bead, rich yet taut, with crisp acidity and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after its long tirage; it can be kept some years more, the toast deepening as the citrus recedes.
wine.serve: 9 to 12 degrees Celsius, as for a fuller, long aged sparkling wine; no decanting; a tulip shaped white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The house's vintage cuvée: every grape grown in the one year printed on the label.
The island's one Geographical Indication, which covers the whole state.

records.table: Six years and more on its lees lend Grand Vintage its weight: the vintage cuvée of House of Arras, founded in 1995 and known for long aged Tasmanian sparkling wine, it is Chardonnay led, with Pinot Noir, and tastes of grapefruit, oyster shell and brioche, enough for a main course.
records.story: The house grew from a visit to Tasmania in 1988 by a sparkling winemaker who saw in the island's cool, maritime climate a home for traditional method wine; in the early 1990s he joined the Hardy wine company. In 1995 BRL Hardy set up a new venture within the company to make sparkling wine from Tasmanian fruit, and it took the name Arras, a word for a rich tapestry: the house's way of saying that its wines are woven from many Tasmanian sites. The first Arras wine, a Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of the 1995 harvest that grew into the Grand Vintage, was released in 1999 after years on its lees, and long tirage became the mark of the house. Above it the house later added a late disgorged release, held on its lees for a decade and more. The label passed with its parent from the Hardy wine company through the Accolade group, and in 2023 Accolade sold House of Arras, with the Bay of Fires winery and cellar door at Pipers River, to the family owned Handpicked Wines. In each Grand Vintage the island's high natural acidity comes rounded by years on the lees, the patience the house is known for.

Australia sets no minimum time on lees comparable to Champagne's; the long tirage of the Grand Vintage is the house's choice, not a rule.

wine.name: Jansz Premium Cuvée
wine.grapes: Chardonnay, usually the larger part, with Pinot Noir; the split moves between releases, and some have held a touch of Meunier.
wine.sites: The estate vineyard at Pipers River on rich, free draining basalt soils, first planted in 1975 under the name Heemskerk, with fruit from other Tasmanian vineyards.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method, which the house calls méthode Tasmanoise: a non vintage blend of base wines given its second fermentation in the bottle, then at least eighteen months on its lees before disgorging, as the house states.
wine.glass: Honeysuckle, lemon zest and fresh strawberry over nougat and roasted nuts from the lees; a creamy mousse, bright acidity and a clean, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink on release, and at its liveliest while the fruit is fresh; it is not a wine built for long cellaring.

records.table: A partnership of 1986 with Louis Roederer began Jansz Tasmania at Pipers River, and Premium Cuvée, its non vintage, is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir given eighteen months and more on lees: honeysuckle, lemon zest and a creamy mousse; open it with oysters.
records.story: The name looks back to the Dutch navigator Abel Janszoon Tasman (about 1603 to 1659), who reached the island's west coast in November 1642 in his ship the Heemskerck. In 1975 a vineyard was planted at Pipers River in the cool north east and named Heemskerk after that ship. In 1986 the Champagne house Louis Roederer, drawn by a climate like that of north east France and by the free draining basalt soils, went into partnership with Heemskerk Wines and planted Chardonnay and Pinot Noir there for traditional method sparkling wine alone; the wine took the name Jansz, from Tasman's patronymic. Roederer was a founding partner and did not stay. In 1998 the Hill-Smith family, the South Australian family behind Yalumba, bought the brand and the property and built it as Jansz Tasmania, a family owned house devoted to sparkling wine. The house coined its own term, méthode Tasmanoise, for the traditional method made in its island way. The Premium Cuvée, its non vintage, is the bottle by which most guests meet Tasmanian sparkling wine, and it shows the island's high acidity softened by time on the lees.

wine.name: Pipers Brook Riesling
wine.sites: Close planted estate vineyards of old Riesling vines in the Pipers Brook district, on red volcanic Ferrosol soils, the krasnozem, in a cool maritime climate near Bass Strait.
wine.making: As the house tells it, the pressed juice has a short time on its skins for aroma and texture, then ferments slowly at very low temperatures in stainless steel vessels, the house says to keep all its freshness.
wine.glass: Lime juice, Meyer lemon and green apple over kaffir lime leaf and a chalky, talc like texture; taut and steely, with fine acidity and a long, zesty finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and taut on release, it keeps for five to ten years and beyond by the house's notes.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for its perfume.

records.table: Steely in the manner of Alsace, the Riesling of Pipers Brook Vineyard, planted by its own account in 1974 in Tasmania's cool north east, comes from old vines on red volcanic soil and is fermented cold in steel: lime, Meyer lemon and chalk, with a long, zesty finish.
records.story: Tasmania's modern vineyards began in the 1950s, with La Provence at Lalla in the north in 1956 and Moorilla Estate near Hobart in 1958. In 1974, by the house's own account, two brothers planted Pipers Brook Vineyard in the cool, maritime country near Pipers River, close to Bass Strait. The house says its sites were chosen for a terroir that recalls the cool wine regions of France, and its Riesling was modelled from the first on the steely, complex Rieslings of Alsace. At the turn of the century the estate changed hands: Kreglinger, a Belgian family trading company, took a majority in 2000 or 2001 by the accounts read, and the estate has traded since as Kreglinger Wine Estates. In 2024 the vineyard marked fifty years since its first planting. Lime and chalk, close planted vines and high acidity: in its Riesling the estate puts the north east's argument plainly, glass by glass.

wine.name: Tolpuddle Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The one vineyard, a gently sloping north east facing site rising from Back Tea Tree Road in the cool, dry Coal River Valley, on light silica over sandstone.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is fermented as whole berries with a share of whole bunches, about half in recent years and some forty per cent in others, in open wooden and stainless steel fermenters; the wine then spends about ten months in French oak, about a third of it new.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and wild strawberry over violet, aniseed, star anise and cracked pepper from the whole bunches; fine, detailed tannin and a long, bright line of acidity.
wine.ageing: Fragrant within a few years of the vintage, it repays cellaring for a decade and more, up to twelve years by the house's notes.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly for its perfume, or not at all; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Whole bunches and French oak go into the red of one Coal River Valley site, planted in 1988 and named for the Tolpuddle Martyrs: Tolpuddle Pinot Noir, dark cherry, violet and star anise over fine, detailed tannin.
records.story: In 1834 six Dorset farm labourers were transported for forming an agricultural union, and the vineyard is named for them, the Tolpuddle Martyrs. Their leader, George Loveless (1797 to 1874), a ploughman and Wesleyan preacher, reached Van Diemen's Land that year and was set to work as a shepherd and stock keeper on the government's domain farm at New Town; pardoned, he sailed for England in 1837. The vineyard was planted in 1988 by a small group of growers and winemakers on a gently sloping, north east facing site in the dry Coal River Valley, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. In 2011 the cousins behind Shaw + Smith, the Adelaide Hills house, bought it, and since then the freshly picked grapes have crossed Bass Strait to be made at their South Australian winery, while the wine keeps the vineyard's name rather than theirs. From one site it makes the Coal River Valley's claim on Pinot Noir: a red grown on a cool island and ripened in a warm, dry valley.

wine.name: Domaine A Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small parts of Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot in the vintages read.
wine.sites: The estate's own Stoney Vineyard at Campania, first planted in 1973, in the dry Coal River Valley north of Hobart.
wine.making: Matured in French oak barrels in a temperature controlled cellar for up to three years, then bottled at the winery and aged there for up to a decade before release, as the house tells it.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and cedar over tobacco leaf, clove and brick dust; firm, fine tannin and fresh, cool climate acidity, more savoury than sweet.
wine.ageing: Released with years of bottle age and open on release, it keeps for many years more, the fruit giving way to cedar and tobacco.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Up to three years in French oak, and years more in bottle, come before Domaine A releases its Cabernet Sauvignon, made in the Bordeaux mould on a Coal River Valley estate founded in 1989: cassis, cedar and tobacco over firm, fine tannin. An older bottle wants decanting.
records.story: The Stoney Vineyard at Campania, north of Hobart, was first planted in 1973 by a local couple, early in the modern wine history of the Coal River Valley. In 1989 a Swiss couple bought it and founded Domaine A there, with the aim of making wines inspired by Bordeaux on a cool island in the Southern Ocean; the dry, warm valley gave them a chance of ripening Cabernet Sauvignon. They kept the Stoney Vineyard name for a second label and gave the Domaine A label to the wines they judged built for long life. Their method was patience: up to three years in French oak, then up to a decade in bottle at the winery before release, so that the wine reached the market with its tannin already settled. The estate came to be known as one of the island's idiosyncratic houses, its Cabernet more European in its acid and structure than most of Australia's. In 2018, looking to retire, the couple sold Domaine A to the owner of Moorilla Estate, near Hobart, and its care passed to Moorilla's winemaker. Savoury, firm and released old, the Cabernet answers anyone who doubts that Bordeaux grapes belong in Tasmania.
